name: Historical English Units of Measurement (pre-1824)
title: Historical English Units of Measurement (pre-1824)
description: Traditional English units of length, area, liquid volume and avoirdupois mass used in England before the 1824 imperial system, with approximate SI equivalents, definitions and origins.

7.92 inches or one 100th of a chain. (A modern Indian surveyor's chain has 200 mm links.)
Width of the outstretched hand, from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger: 9 inches (= 3 palms).

Prior to the Anglo-Saxon invasions, the Roman foot of 11.65 inches (296 mm) was used. The Anglo-Saxons introduced a North-German foot of 13.2 inches (335 mm), divided into 4 palms or 12 thumbs, while the Roman foot continued to be used in the construction crafts. In the late 13th century, the modern foot of 304.8 mm was introduced, equal to exactly 10 ⁄ 11 Anglo-Saxon foot.
From fingertips to elbow, 18 inches.
3 feet = 36 inches, the practical base unit, defined as the length of the prototype bar held by the Crown or Exchequer.
From fingertip of outstretched arm to opposite shoulder, 20 nails = 1 + 1 ⁄ 4 yard or 45 inches. Mostly for measuring cloth.
6 feet, distance between arms outstretched, from fingertip to fingertip, on a 6-foot-tall person.

Also called a perch or pole: a measure used for surveying land and in architecture. The length of the rod (then called perch) was declared to be 16 + 1 ⁄ 2 feet or 5 + 1 ⁄ 2 yards in the Composition of Yards and Perches. The square pole is commonly used as a measurement for Allotment gardens. (See also perch as an area and a volume unit.) It may have originated from the typical length of a medieval ox-goad.
rows.origin_or_usage: Likely agricultural, could be from surveying

rows.definition: Four linear rods. Named after the length of surveyor's chain used to measure distances until quite recently. Any of several actual chains used for land surveying and divided in links. Gunter's chain, introduced in the 17th century, is 66 feet (20.1 metres).
A textile measurement, defined typically as 96 ells, or a sixth of a hank.

Notionally the distance a plough team could furrow without rest, but actually a measure of 40 rods or 600 feet prior to the Composition of Yards and Perches; 40 rods or 660 feet since then. (See also the Ancient Greek stadion or 'stade'.)
A textile measurement, composed of 6 skeins.

5280 feet or 1760 yards. Originally the Roman mile, 1000 paces, later reckoned as 5000 feet, but adjusted to 5280 feet in 1593 to account for the differences introduced to these methods of reckoning by the Composition of Yards and Perches.
Notionally an hour's march, but usually reckoned as three miles. Approximate length of the traditional "mile" in German and Scandinavian countries.
A textile measurement for cotton and linen, composed of 20 hanks.

30.25 square yards. A square rod is also known as a square pole or a square perch. Sometimes the word 'square' is omitted when the context clearly indicates that the subject is area, notably so in the case of British allotment gardens.
One quarter of an acre; one 'furlong' in length by one 'rod' in width; 40 square 'rods'. The rood was sometimes called an acre itself in many ancient contexts.

An area of land one chain (four rods) wide by one furlong in length. As the traditional furlong could vary in length from country to country, so did the acre. In England an acre was 4,840 square yards (4,050 m 2), in Scotland 6,150 square yards (5,140 m 2) and in Ireland 7,840 square yards (6,560 m 2). It is a Saxon unit, meaning "field".
The area that one ox can plough in a single year. Approximately 15 acres or one eighth of a carucate.
The area that a pair of oxen can plough in a single year. Approximately 30 acres (also called yard land).
The area that can be ploughed by one eight-oxen team in a single year (also called a plough or carve). Approximately 120 acres.
Also known as a drop.
